source.version: PsyArXiv/OSF preprint v1, posted 2024-05-28 (https://osf.io/vzu3c/); primary file 'Open and Closed-Ended Problem Solving in Humans and AI.docx', modified 2024-05-28, OSF file ID 665605af65e1de4562893d5a. Read the entire document, references, Appendices A-C, and embedded figures in memory; converted the DOCX to a 72-page PDF with PyMuPDF to verify numeric text. All page locators refer to that rendering. The journal version of record (Thinking Skills and Creativity 53, 101598, 2024) was not read. OSF API metadata confirms version and posting date. OpenAlex returns a complete abstract_inverted_index; Crossref returns no abstract.
source.title_on_document: Open and Closed-Ended Problem Solving in Humans and AI: The Influence of Question Asking Complexity

supplement.where: OSF: https://osf.io/hsxza/?view_only=35d6f9266e9c4c2fad6ca12840500017 (p. 13, Transparency and openness; p. 50, Data availability). Appendices A (stumpers), B (CPS dilemmas and instructions), and C (GPT prompts) are inside the document, pp. 65-72.
supplement.holds: Data, analysis scripts, and weights for the scoring models. The main text already prints arm means, SDs, t statistics, and d for every AI-versus-human comparison.

paper_design_summary: Studies 1 (Prolific, 89 analyzed) and 2 (Prolific, 100 reported) examined correlations between question-asking complexity and originality (AQT), closed-ended riddles (stumpers), the AUT, and open-ended creative problem solving (CPS). No people were randomly assigned to AI assistance; the order of AQT objects and stumpers (Study 1) or CPS dilemmas (Study 2) was randomized within unaided human tasks. Study 3 generated 100 GPT-4 instances, using separate sessions per task, and compared the scored AI outputs with the human responses from Studies 1 and 2 (pp. 13-18, 25-26, 32-37).

ai_tool.how_used: The first author prompted GPT-4 in separate sessions per task (AQT, stumpers, CPS, AUT); GPT-4 was told to give 5-7 answers on the AQT and AUT to match human fluency. No person received AI help.

task.description: AQT, AUT, 15 stumpers, and five CPS dilemmas, as administered to humans in Studies 1 and 2.

outcomes.name: CPS solution originality
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Fine-tuned GPT-2 scorer of CPS originality (Luchini et al., 2023), scale 1-5, averaged per participant or GPT-4 session.

contrasts.reported: GPT-4 did not differ significantly in CPS originality (M = 2.28, SD = 0.32) from human participants (M = 2.2, SD = 0.37), t(100) = 0.75, p = .46, d = 0.151

eligibility.reason: No people were randomly assigned to AI assistance. Studies 1 and 2 are correlational studies of unaided humans; AQT object and stumper/CPS item order was randomized within unaided tasks (pp. 18 and 26, Procedures). Their human samples meet the size threshold: Study 1 analyzed 89 people and Study 2 reports 100, with no numerical exclusion count (pp. 2, 13 and 25-27). Originality, complexity, quality, and accuracy were scored on produced responses (pp. 15-18 and 26). Study 3 compares GPT-4 outputs with those human samples; its 100 artificial instances are not people and do not establish eligibility (pp. 32-34, Methods; pp. 36-37, AI vs. Humans). Core remains no; context_class remains ai_vs_human.

one_line_finding: GPT-4 (100 sessions) beat Prolific participants on AUT originality (3.28 vs 2.22, d = 3.25) and CPS solution quality (3.6 vs 2.82, d = 2.36), but CPS solution originality did not differ (2.28 vs 2.2, t(100) = 0.75, p = .46) (OSF preprint, Study 3, AI vs. Humans, pp. 36-37).
open_questions: The AI vs. Humans prose and Figures 5-6 disagree on several means (pp. 36-37; detailed in notes). Which values are authoritative remains unresolved; the form retains the prose statistics, and the journal full text was not read.

All AI-versus-human comparisons print t(100), while the methods separately report 100 GPT-4 instances and human samples of 89 and 100. The outcome-specific analysis counts and degrees of freedom require clarification; no combined N or replacement statistic has been inferred (pp. 13, 25, 33, 36-37).
notes: Locators are page numbers of the pymupdf rendering of the OSF preprint docx, not of the journal article; numbers could differ in the version of record. The paper prints t(100) for every AI-versus-human comparison, although the groups hold 100 GPT-4 sessions and 89 or 100 people; recorded as printed. Treatment and control are labels only: the AI-versus-human contrast puts GPT-4 in the treatment slot. All recorded AI-versus-human statistics and the one-line finding use the AI vs. Humans results prose on pp. 36-37. The combined outcome-specific analysis counts are not printed, so n_units is null; human sample sizes and AI instance counts remain separate. The figure images were inspected directly from the DOCX in memory. Figure 5 (p. 36; word/media/image8.png) labels GPT-4/human AUT means 3.27/2.23, whereas the prose gives 3.28/2.22; GPT-4 complexity is 4.50 in the figure versus 4.51 in prose; human stumper accuracy is 3.94 versus 3.9. Figure 6 (p. 37; word/media/image9.png) labels human AQT originality 0.90 versus 0.89 in prose; GPT-4/human complexity 4.50/3.41 versus 4.51/3.40; AUT 3.27/2.33 versus 3.28/2.32; CPS quality 3.60/2.84 versus 3.6/2.82; and CPS originality 2.29/2.21 versus 2.28/2.2. Some discrepancies exceed simple rounding; figure values have not been substituted for prose values. Study 2 comparisons for AUT and AQT originality are separate contrasts, not variants of the scoring measures. The same GPT-4 sample is reused across comparisons. Availability = mixed describes AI-generated versus unaided-human outputs, not human access to AI. Neither a delayed post-AI assessment nor an outcome explicitly designated primary is reported. The data/code URL is the repository cited by the paper; its contents were not audited.

Some discrepancies exceed simple rounding; figure values have not been substituted for prose values. Study 2 comparisons for AUT and AQT originality are separate contrasts, not variants of the scoring measures. The same GPT-4 sample is reused across comparisons.
